questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: C.1 (Simple harmonic motion: period of a mass-spring system) and experimental skills
questions.subtopic: C.1 Simple harmonic motion — data-based question
questions.challenge_mechanism: The relationship is only visible after a non-obvious linearisation, and one row has been seeded with a genuine experimental fault that a best-fit line will expose but a naive endpoint calculation will absorb silently.

stimulus.title: Student investigation: the period of a loaded spring
stimulus.body: A student hangs a spring from a rigid support and suspends a mass hanger from its lower end. She pulls the hanger a short distance below its equilibrium position and releases it, so that the system oscillates vertically. She measures the time for 20 complete oscillations using a stopwatch that reads to 0.01 s, and divides by 20 to obtain the period. She estimates her reaction time as 0.2 s at both the start and the stop. She repeats the measurement for seven different loads. The masses are known to the nearest gram, so the uncertainty in the load is negligible.

table.caption: Measured period for each load. One row in the table is unreliable.

questions.question: The student intends to test the relationship $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$ and to determine the spring constant $k$ from her data.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the uncertainty in a single value of the period $T$, and explain how you obtained it from the information given about the timing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student could reduce the uncertainty in the period using the same stopwatch, and state one further change to the apparatus that would reduce it more.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the student should plot a graph of $T^2$ against $m$ rather than $T$ against $m$, and state what feature of the resulting graph would support the proposed relationship.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the spring constant $k$ from the data. You should make it clear which points you used to fix your best-fit line and why, and give $k$ with its unit.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Evaluate whether the data support the proposed relationship. Identify any anomalous reading, suggest a plausible experimental cause for it, and state what the student should have done at the time.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The reaction time contributes at both the start and the stop, so combining in quadrature gives $\Delta t = \sqrt{0.2^2 + 0.2^2} = 0.28\ \mathrm{s}$ for the timing of 20 oscillations. Since $T = t/20$, the uncertainty in the period is $\Delta T = 0.28/20 = 0.014\ \mathrm{s}$. **(M1)** for dividing the timing uncertainty by the number of oscillations, **(A1)** for a value of about $0.01\ \mathrm{s}$ to $0.02\ \mathrm{s}$. Adding the two reaction times directly instead of in quadrature gives $0.4/20 = 0.020\ \mathrm{s}$, which is also acceptable; the stopwatch resolution of $0.01\ \mathrm{s}$ is far smaller than either and can be ignored.

**(b)** Timing a larger number of oscillations divides the same timing uncertainty by a larger number, so 50 oscillations rather than 20 would give $\Delta T \approx 0.006\ \mathrm{s}$. **(A1)** A much larger reduction comes from removing the human element: a position sensor or a video recording analysed frame by frame gives a period limited only by the sampling rate. **(A1)** Note that timing more oscillations is free, which is why it should always be the first thing a student does.

**(c)** The relationship $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ is not linear in $m$, so a graph of $T$ against $m$ would be a curve and a curve cannot confirm a hypothesis by eye. Squaring gives $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{k}\,m$, which is the equation of a straight line through the origin with gradient $4\pi^2/k$. **(M1)** The relationship is supported if the plotted points lie close to a straight line **(A1)** and if that line passes through, or very close to, the origin **(A1)** — a non-zero intercept would indicate that the spring's own mass is contributing to the inertia of the system.

**(d)** The point at $m = 0.300\ \mathrm{kg}$ lies well above the trend and must be excluded from the fit **(R1)**; the reason is given in part (e). Using the remaining six points, a least-squares fit of $T^2$ against $m$ gives a gradient of $1.56\ \mathrm{s^2\ kg^{-1}}$ and an intercept of about $0.005\ \mathrm{s^2}$, effectively zero. **(M1)** Hence $k = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{\text{gradient}} = \dfrac{39.5}{1.56} = 25.3\ \mathrm{N\ m^{-1}}$. **(A1)** A hand-drawn best-fit line will give a gradient anywhere in the range $1.53$ to $1.60\ \mathrm{s^2\ kg^{-1}}$, so any value of $k$ from $24.7$ to $25.8\ \mathrm{N\ m^{-1}}$ should be credited. **(A1)**

**(e)** With the anomalous point removed, the remaining six points lie on a straight line through the origin to within the scatter expected from the timing uncertainty, so the data do support the relationship. **(A1)** The reading at $m = 0.300\ \mathrm{kg}$ is the anomalous one: the model predicts $T = 2\pi\sqrt{0.300/25} = 0.688\ \mathrm{s}$, whereas $0.730\ \mathrm{s}$ was recorded, some $6\%$ high, which is far outside the $2\%$ timing uncertainty at that load. **(M1)** A plausible cause is that the hanger caught on the support or that an extra mass was left on the hanger for that run. The student should have repeated that measurement immediately, while the apparatus was still set up, rather than processing a single suspicious value. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes: In (a) accept any value from 0.014 s to 0.020 s; credit the method of dividing by 20 even if the combination of the two reaction times is done by simple addition. Do not credit the stopwatch resolution of 0.01 s alone, which ignores the dominant error. In (b) the first mark is for timing more oscillations; the second must be a change of technique, not simply 'be more careful' or 'use a better stopwatch'. In (c) all three marks are for the linearisation argument: award the first for stating that the untransformed graph is curved, the second for the straight-line prediction, and the third for the through-the-origin test. In (d) allow follow-through from a gradient obtained with the anomalous point included, provided the point is not silently absorbed; a candidate who includes it and comments on the resulting poor fit can still earn the reasoning marks. In (e) the anomaly must be identified by its load, and the suggested cause must be physically plausible rather than 'human error' alone. A candidate who argues that the point should simply be deleted without a reason earns no credit.
questions.explanation: This item is built around a distinction that Paper 1B rewards and that coursework often does not: the difference between calculating a result and interrogating a dataset. The linearisation in (c) is the first hurdle, and it is the one that separates candidates who treat a graph as a formality from those who use it as a test — a curve can be fitted to almost anything, and only a straight line lets you judge a hypothesis by eye. The seeded anomaly in (d) and (e) is the second hurdle, and it is deliberately placed in the middle of the range rather than at an end, so that an endpoint calculation absorbs it silently while a best-fit line exposes it: a candidate who uses only the first and last rows obtains a gradient of about 1.55 and never notices anything is wrong, whereas one who plots the points sees immediately that the fifth sits above the trend. The final trap is in (e), where the natural answer is to delete the point and move on; what the markscheme wants is a stated physical cause and the correct experimental response, which is to repeat the measurement at once rather than to discard inconvenient data after the fact.  A further check that this dataset invites, and that examiners return to, is the intercept. Had the best-fit line cut the T squared axis clearly above zero, the natural conclusion would be that the spring's own mass is oscillating along with the load, contributing roughly one third of its mass to the effective inertia. The data here were generated with a negligible intercept so that this complication does not obscure the main test, but a candidate who comments on the size of the intercept rather than ignoring it is displaying exactly the judgement Paper 1B is designed to reward.

provenance.adaptation: Original dataset generated in Python from T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k) with k = 25.0 N per metre, then perturbed by up to 1.2 per cent and rounded to the resolution implied by timing 20 oscillations. The row at 0.300 kg was deliberately raised by 6 per cent to sit well outside the timing uncertainty while remaining physically plausible.

verification.method: Dataset generated in Python from the stated model with a known spring constant, then rounded to the measurement resolution; the seeded anomaly was confirmed to lie well outside the timing uncertainty and the least-squares gradient excluding it was checked against the analytic value 4 pi squared over k.
solution_skeleton: combine the reaction-time uncertainties and divide by the number of oscillations
square the model to linearise it and identify the gradient
fit a best-fit line excluding the anomalous point
take the gradient and invert it to recover the spring constant
test the intercept against zero and judge whether the model is supported

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: E.3 (Radioactive decay: detection of radiation, counting statistics) and experimental skills
questions.topic: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
questions.challenge_mechanism: The exponent has to be extracted from a log-log graph rather than assumed, one reading carries a seeded systematic fault that a residual plot exposes, and the uncertainty is not a stated instrument limit but has to be derived from counting statistics.

stimulus.title: Student investigation: count rate and distance from a source
stimulus.body: A student places a sealed gamma source on a metre rule and a Geiger-Muller tube connected to a counter at a measured distance $d$ from it. At each distance she records the count over 100 s and divides by 100 to obtain the count rate. The background count rate was measured separately, over 600 s, as 0.40 counts per second, and has already been subtracted from the values in the table. The distances were set with a metre rule graduated in millimetres. One reading in the table is unreliable.

table.caption: Background-corrected count rate at each distance.

questions.question: The student wants to find the exponent $n$ in the relationship $C = \dfrac{A}{d^{\,n}}$, where $A$ is a constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The count recorded at $d = 20.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ over 100 s was 10200. Assuming the counts follow Poisson statistics, calculate the percentage uncertainty in this count rate, and state what the uncertainty would have been had the count been recorded over only 10 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the background count rate was measured over 600 s rather than 100 s, and explain why subtracting the background before analysing the data matters more at large distances than at small ones.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how plotting $\lg C$ against $\lg d$ allows the exponent $n$ and the constant $A$ to be found, and state what the gradient and the intercept represent.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the exponent $n$ and the constant $A$, making clear which point you excluded and giving the unit of $A$.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Evaluate whether the data confirm the inverse-square relationship. Identify the anomalous reading, suggest a plausible cause, and state what should have been done about it.

questions.answer:
**(a)** For a Poisson count, the uncertainty in the number of counts is $\sqrt{N}$, so with $N = 10200$ the uncertainty is $101$ counts and the percentage uncertainty is $\dfrac{101}{10200} \times 100 = 0.99\%$, which is also $1/\sqrt{N}$ expressed as a percentage. **(M1)(A1)** Over 10 s the same rate would give $N = 1020$ counts, so the percentage uncertainty would be $1/\sqrt{1020} \times 100 = 3.1\%$. **(A1)** The uncertainty therefore improves only as the square root of the counting time, which is why long counts are needed for precision.

**(b)** The background rate is small, so it must be known precisely before it can be subtracted; a 600 s count gives $N \approx 240$ counts and hence a percentage uncertainty of about $1/\sqrt{240} = 6\%$, whereas a 100 s count would give only 40 counts and around $16\%$. **(A1)** Subtracting the background matters far more at large distances because the corrected rate there is small: at $d = 50\ \mathrm{cm}$ the measured rate is 16 per second, so a background uncertainty of even a few per cent is comparable with the quantity being measured, while at $d = 10\ \mathrm{cm}$ the rate of 403 per second makes the same background correction negligible. **(A1)**

**(c)** Taking logarithms of $C = A/d^{\,n}$ gives $\lg C = \lg A - n\,\lg d$, which is the equation of a straight line. **(M1)** The gradient is $-n$, so the exponent is found directly from the slope **(A1)**, and the intercept on the $\lg C$ axis is $\lg A$, from which $A$ follows as $10^{\text{intercept}}$ **(A1)**. This is the only straightforward way to test the value of an exponent, since a direct plot of $C$ against $d$ is a curve whose shape is very hard to judge by eye.

**(d)** The point at $d = 30.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ sits clearly above the trend and must be excluded from the fit **(R1)**; part (e) gives the reason. Using the remaining six points, a least-squares fit of $\lg C$ against $\lg d$ gives a gradient of $-1.99$ and an intercept of $4.60$. **(M1)** Hence $n = 1.99 \approx 2.0$ **(A1)** and $A = 10^{4.60} = 4.0 \times 10^4\ \mathrm{s^{-1}\ cm^{2}}$, with the unit fixed by the requirement that $A/d^2$ has the unit of a count rate. **(A1)** A hand-drawn line will give $n$ in the range $1.9$ to $2.1$ and $A$ in the range $3.5$ to $4.5 \times 10^4\ \mathrm{s^{-1}\ cm^2}$; all such values should be credited.

**(e)** With the anomalous point removed, the remaining six points lie on a straight line of gradient $-2.0$ to within the counting uncertainties, so the data do confirm the inverse-square relationship. **(A1)** The anomalous reading is at $d = 30.0\ \mathrm{cm}$: the fitted relationship predicts $C = 4.0 \times 10^4/30^2 = 44\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, whereas $57\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ was recorded, roughly $28\%$ high and many times the $1.5\%$ counting uncertainty at that rate. **(M1)** A plausible cause is that the source was not properly seated against the rule for that reading, so the true distance was smaller than 30.0 cm. The student should have rechecked the alignment and repeated the measurement immediately rather than carrying a suspicious value forward into the analysis. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes: In (a) accept any value from 0.98 to 1.0 per cent for the 100 s count and 3.0 to 3.2 per cent for the 10 s count; the key relationship being tested is that the uncertainty scales as one over the square root of the number of counts. In (b) the first mark is for linking a longer background count to a smaller percentage uncertainty; the second must refer explicitly to the corrected rate being small at large distances, and 'because the count rate is smaller' on its own is not sufficient. In (c) award the first mark for the logarithmic transformation, the second for the gradient being minus n, and the third for the intercept being the logarithm of A. In (d) allow follow-through from a gradient that includes the anomalous point only if the candidate comments on the resulting poor fit; a silent inclusion earns no reasoning mark. The unit of A must be consistent with the unit of d used, and a candidate who works in metres should have A of order 4.0 per second per square metre, which is equally acceptable. In (e) the anomaly must be identified by its distance, and 'the source moved' is acceptable only if the direction of the resulting error is stated correctly.
questions.explanation: Two ideas make this item hard, and both are examined regularly in Paper 1B. The first is that an exponent cannot be read off a curve: a plot of count rate against distance looks like 'some kind of decay' for any inverse power, and only a logarithmic plot turns the exponent into a number that can be measured and compared with a prediction. The second is that the uncertainty here is not written on an instrument but has to be derived from the counts themselves, which is why part (a) asks for it before any graph is drawn; a candidate who does not realise that precision improves only as the square root of counting time will not see why the 100 s count was worth the trouble. The seeded anomaly at 30 cm is placed where it does the most damage: it is in the middle of the range, so it pulls a hand-drawn line without producing an obviously wild point, and because the counting statistics at that rate are good, the discrepancy cannot be waved away as random scatter. The final mark is reserved for the experimental response — repeating the measurement then and there, rather than deleting a point afterwards — because that is the habit the question exists to reward.  It is also worth being explicit about why the background has to be removed before the logarithms are taken. Subtracting a constant from C is not the same operation as subtracting a constant from the logarithm of C, so a candidate who plots the raw count rates and tries to correct the result afterwards obtains a gradient that drifts steadily with distance and will conclude that the exponent itself is changing. The data here are given already corrected, so the log-log plot is clean, and the underlying point is tested directly in part (b) instead, where it can be assessed on its own.

provenance.adaptation: Original dataset generated in Python from C = A/d^2 with A = 4.0 x 10^4 per second per square centimetre, perturbed by up to 3 per cent and rounded to whole counts. The row at 30.0 cm was deliberately raised by 28 per cent so that it lies far outside the counting uncertainty while remaining a plausible consequence of the source being misaligned.

verification.method: Dataset generated in Python from the inverse-square model with known parameters and rounded to whole counts; the least-squares log-log gradient was checked against minus two both with and without the seeded anomaly, and every uncertainty derived from the square-root-of-N rule was recomputed independently.
solution_skeleton: derive the counting uncertainty from the square root of the number of counts
take logarithms of the power-law model to linearise it
fit the log-log line excluding the anomalous point
read the exponent from the gradient and the constant from the intercept
compare the fitted prediction with the suspect reading and name a cause
